text: There was a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Micah.

He said to his mother, "The eleven hundred pieces of silver that were taken from you—about which you uttered a curse and spoke it in my hearing—look, the silver is with me; I took it." His mother said, "May the LORD bless you, my son."

versions.text: He said to his mother, "The eleven hundred pieces of silver that were taken from you—about which you uttered a curse in my hearing—I took that silver; it is with me." His mother said, "May the LORD bless you, my son."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two verbs ("you uttered a curse and also spoke it in my hearing"), and the confession follows the order "the silver is with me; I took it," with the attention-getting particle hinneh. Restoring the sequence keeps the dramatic force of the son's admission and reads well aloud.

text: He returned the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother, and she said, "I solemnly dedicate this silver to the LORD, from my own hand, for my son, to make a carved image and a cast idol. Now I give it back to you."
So he returned the silver to his mother, and she took two hundred pieces of it and gave them to a silversmith, who made them into a carved image and a cast idol. And it was placed in Micah's house.

versions.text: So he returned the silver to his mother, and she took two hundred pieces of it and gave them to a silversmith, who made them into a carved image and a cast idol. And it stood in Micah's house.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew simply says "and it was in the house of Micah." "Stood" adds a physical posture not in the text; a neutral rendering is more accurate and equally natural to read aloud.

text: This man Micah had a shrine,* and he made an ephod and household idols, and he installed one of his sons to serve him as priest. [*Footnote: Hebrew "a house of God" (or "of gods").]

versions.text: This man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household idols, and he installed one of his sons to serve him as priest.
versions.explanation: "Shrine" is a fair rendering, but a brief footnote giving the literal Hebrew helps readers see the irony of a private "house of God" alongside idols, without changing the readable text.

text: In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did as he saw fit.
Now there was a young man from Bethlehem in Judah, of the clan of Judah. He was a Levite, and he was staying there.
This man left the town of Bethlehem in Judah to find some other place to live. On his way he came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah.
Micah asked him, "Where do you come from?" He answered, "I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am looking for a place to live."
Then Micah said to him, "Stay with me and be my father and priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year, along with a set of clothes and your food." So the Levite went in.

versions.text: Then Micah said to him, "Stay with me and be my father and priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year, along with your clothing and your food." So the Levite went in with him.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads only "and the Levite went (in)." The added "with him" supplies information not present in the text; the shorter form preserves the terse Hebrew and still flows naturally.

versions.text: Then Micah said to him, "Stay with me and be my father and priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year, along with your clothing and your food." So the Levite went in.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew עֵרֶךְ בְּגָדִים denotes a set or outfit of clothing, a specified item in the wage offer. "Your clothing" loses the sense of a measured allowance and blurs the concreteness of the terms Micah offers.

text: The Levite agreed to stay with the man, and the young man became like one of his own sons to him.
Micah installed the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in his house.
Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, since I have a Levite as my priest."
